The LCTR vehicle requires a main-rotor speed range from 650 ft/s in VTOL mode to 350 ft/s in cruise mode, resulting in 50° or more variations in VSPT blade incidence angles.
The transonic turbine cascade facility was modified to accommodate a wider range of incidence angles, from a minimum of -46.5° to a maximum of +29.1°.
The key measurements included total pressure, flow angles, blade and endwall static pressures, and 12 new exit static pressure taps.
At negative incidence angles, the non-uniform exit static pressures were observed, with the blade row and back wall establishing a converging exhaust section.
The exit flow surveys showed significant changes in the total pressure and flow angle distributions with variations in incidence angle and Reynolds number.
The blade loading showed that as the incidence angle became more negative, the suction side pressure coefficient decreased, indicating reduced loading.
The loss levels were observed to decrease with negative incidence and increase with decreasing Reynolds number, resulting in a narrower loss bucket at lower Reynolds numbers.
The exit flow angles also varied significantly with incidence angle and Reynolds number.
The cascade facility was operated over a wide range of Reynolds numbers, from 6.83x10^5 to 0.85x10^5, and two isentropic exit Mach numbers of 0.74 and 0.34.
The key conclusions were that the facility modifications were successful, the data showed good repeatability and consistency, and the dataset provides a valuable case for CFD code validation.
The main technical challenges were accommodating the large incidence angle variations and addressing the transitional Reynolds number effects.
The study supports the development of variable-speed power turbine (VSPT) technology for the NASA Large Civil Tilt Rotor (LCTR) vehicle.
The GE EEE tip section blade with a design inlet angle of 29.7° and design exit angle of 64.4° was used in the study.
Midspan exit total pressure and flow angle measurements were obtained at seven inlet flow angles, ranging from +29.1° to -46.5°.
For each inlet angle, data were obtained at five flow conditions with inlet Reynolds numbers varying from 6.83x10^5 to 0.85x10^5 and two isentropic exit Mach numbers of 0.74 and 0.34.
